PART A
```{r}
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
students

typeof(students$name)
class(students$name)

units = c(3, 3, 2),
instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz"))
```

PART D
```{r}
students$year_level <- c(2, 3, 1, 4, 2)

students[order(students$age), ]
order(-students$age)
```

Question #7
```{r}
#No, since the column no longer exists, it's turned into NULL and itr returns nothing. Keeping track #of the current structure matters because each operation changes the data frame, and later steps can #silently break or give empty results if they rely on columns that are gone.”

#Question #8
# First, R reads students$age. Then order() returns the row positions that would put
# those ages in ascending order (3 1 5 2 4), so the code becomes students[c(3, 1, 5, 2, 4), ].
# R pulls the rows in that sequence. The empty space after the comma means "all columns,"
# so each whole row moves as one unit and every column stays lined up with its age.
```

PART E
```{r}
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)
grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")

grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
```

```{r}
# I would add a change column, then sort by change and by midterm,

```

Conclusion 
```{r}
# A data frame compiles vectors into a single table. It is built on a list, which lets one column
# be text, another numeric, and another logical. This relates to vectors and lists by combining
# the vectors' strict one-type columns with the list's flexibility, which makes storing data
# cleaner and more efficient. Hence it is R's primary structure for real-world tabular data like
# spreadsheets and CSV files, since it supports subsetting, sorting, and adding calculated columns.
```
